title: Valmiki Ramayana: The Story, Seven Kandas and Key Characters
description: Explore the Valmiki Ramayana through a detailed story guide, all seven Kandas, key characters, source references, festivals and RudraNāda music.
dek: A kingdom is left behind, a household is broken apart, and a search crosses the sea. Read the Ramayana through its seven books, the people who carry its decisions, and the sources behind the stories.
summary: The Valmiki Ramayana is a Sanskrit epic traditionally attributed to the sage Valmiki. It follows Rama, Sita and their companions through exile, abduction, the search for Sita, the war in Lanka and the return to Ayodhya. The received seven-book text also includes earlier histories and the events of Rama’s later reign.

sections.heading: What is the Valmiki Ramayana?
paragraphs: The Ramayana is both a sustained story and a work people have lived with through recitation, worship, theatre, music and argument. Its central journey follows Rama of Ayodhya, his wife Sita and his brother Lakshmana into exile. When Ravana abducts Sita, the search for her brings Rama into alliance with Sugriva, Hanuman and the vanara forces. Their campaign reaches Lanka and ends with Ravana’s defeat and the royal family’s return.

That outline is useful, but it leaves much out. The poem repeatedly asks what happens when love, a promise, public responsibility and personal judgment make conflicting demands. A father’s word changes his son’s future. A brother refuses a throne. A captive refuses her captor. An ally must be reminded of a promise after regaining power. Victory itself does not make every wound disappear.

Valmiki’s Sanskrit Ramayana is a foundational telling of this story, not a container into which every later Ramayana episode can be placed. Tulsidas’s Ramcharitmanas, Kamban’s Ramavataram, regional performance traditions and many other works have their own language, theology, emphasis and narrative choices. This guide concentrates on Valmiki and names other traditions when they enter the discussion.

The received text is arranged in seven Kandas, or books, divided into sargas, or chapters. A traditional description speaks of 24,000 verses, but exact counts and divisions vary by edition. A reference such as Kishkindha Kanda 66 is useful only if the reader also knows which arrangement of the text is being used.

sections.heading: Valmiki, the poem’s singers and the editions used here
paragraphs: In the opening frame, Valmiki asks Narada to identify a person who possesses an exceptional combination of qualities. Narada answers with Rama’s name and an outline of his life. Valmiki’s response to the killing of a bird becomes the occasion for the first metrical utterance in the poem’s account of its own origin. Brahma then authorizes the telling.

Lava and Kusha appear as singers of the epic. Their presence at the beginning looks forward to the later account of their recitation before Rama. The story therefore gives itself a setting in listening and performance. Rama’s life becomes something that can be remembered, sung and heard by Rama himself.

Traditional attribution to Valmiki and the scholarly study of textual development are different kinds of inquiry. The surviving text has been transmitted through manuscripts and recensions, and modern editors compare those witnesses. A Critical Edition is the result of that work; it is not a recovered autograph in the poet’s hand.

For books one to six, the Kanda guides use the chapter numbering in the Sanskrit-and-English presentation at [ValmikiRamayan.net](https://www.valmikiramayan.net/), translated by Desiraju Hanumanta Rao and K. M. K. Murthy. For Uttara Kanda they use Hari Prasad Shastri’s main chapter numbering, with his supplementary lettered chapters identified. Scholarly discussion of the seventh book is linked separately. These sources are not presented as one uniform edition.

Each guide provides a narrative and a chapter-range reading map. It is an original explanatory companion to the text, not a full translation or a commentary on every verse. The source links let you move from the account here to the passages being discussed.

sections.heading: The story begins: birth, education and marriage
paragraphs: Dasharatha rules Ayodhya but lacks an heir. The opening book describes the royal sacrifices, the divine purpose associated with Vishnu’s human birth and the births of four brothers: Rama, Bharata, Lakshmana and Shatrughna. Their mothers are Kausalya, Kaikeyi and Sumitra. The affection among the brothers gives the later separation its emotional weight.

Rama’s first journey out of the palace is with Vishvamitra, accompanied by Lakshmana. He protects the sage’s sacrifice, learns the use and withdrawal of divine weapons, confronts Tataka and encounters a world whose histories are told along the road. Vishvamitra’s own transformation from king to brahmarshi occupies a substantial part of the book.

At Mithila, Rama breaks Shiva’s bow and marries Sita, whom Janaka has raised as his daughter. The other three brothers also marry. An encounter with Parashurama occurs on the journey afterward, before the family returns to Ayodhya. [Bala Kanda](/ramayana/bala-kanda) includes these events as well as the stories of Ganga, Bhagiratha, Ahalya, Trishanku and Shunahshepa. They form the world around the principal narrative.

sections.heading: Why Rama leaves Ayodhya
paragraphs: Dasharatha prepares to install Rama as heir. Kaikeyi, persuaded by Manthara, invokes two earlier promises: Bharata must receive the position, and Rama must spend fourteen years in the forest. Rama accepts the exile as binding upon him through his father’s word. The decision is not painless or unanimously welcomed. Kausalya grieves and Lakshmana objects fiercely.

Sita insists on accompanying Rama after he first proposes that she remain in the city. Lakshmana also chooses to go. They leave behind not only wealth but the people whose daily lives have been arranged around them. Guha and Bharadwaja help them on the journey, and they establish themselves at Chitrakuta.

Dasharatha dies in grief. Bharata returns to learn what has been done in his name and rejects it. He travels to Rama and asks him to come back. Rama refuses to break the exile; Bharata accepts the responsibility of governing with Rama’s sandals as the sign of the absent ruler’s authority. [Ayodhya Kanda](/ramayana/ayodhya-kanda) makes room for the arguments on both sides rather than treating their love as an automatic answer to the dispute.

sections.heading: Forest life becomes a search for Sita
paragraphs: The forest contains settled ascetic communities, hospitality, beauty and conflict. Rama promises to protect the sages, and Sita questions the dangers of carrying weapons and making violence a habit. Their conversation makes the forest book a place of moral inquiry before the central catastrophe arrives.

At Panchavati, the encounter with Shurpanakha leads to her mutilation and to battles with Khara’s forces. Ravana then draws Maricha into a plan to abduct Sita. Maricha becomes the golden deer that attracts Rama away from the dwelling. His imitation of Rama’s voice brings about Lakshmana’s departure, despite his doubts about the cry.

Ravana approaches in disguise and carries Sita away after she rejects him. Jatayu fights to stop the abduction and is mortally wounded. Sita drops ornaments during the journey and continues to resist in Lanka. Rama, finding the dwelling empty, moves through grief, anger and the search for evidence.

Jatayu supplies crucial testimony before dying. Kabandha later directs the brothers toward Sugriva, and they visit Shabari before reaching Pampa. [Aranya Kanda](/ramayana/aranya-kanda) closes with a direction for the search, but no certainty that it will succeed.

sections.heading: Hanuman, Sugriva and the search parties
paragraphs: Hanuman approaches the brothers on Sugriva’s behalf. His first task is to establish who they are and whether they can be trusted. Rama is impressed by his speech. The future leap across the ocean begins, in narrative terms, with an intelligent conversation between strangers.

Rama and Sugriva form an alliance. Sugriva will help find Sita; Rama will help him overcome Vali and recover his position. Vali’s death produces a serious argument about justice within the text, followed by Tara’s grief and concern for Angada. Sugriva’s restoration does not resolve Rama’s loss, and the delay before the search tests their friendship.

Search parties leave in four directions. The southern group eventually meets Sampati, who identifies Lanka as Sita’s location. At the shore, the task seems beyond the party’s capacity. Jambavan recalls Hanuman’s strength, and Hanuman prepares to attempt the crossing. This is the ending of [Kishkindha Kanda](/ramayana/kishkindha-kanda), not yet the beginning of his journey through Lanka.

sections.heading: How Hanuman finds Sita and gains her trust
paragraphs: [Sundara Kanda](/ramayana/sundara-kanda) opens with the crossing. Hanuman responds differently to hospitality, a test and a hostile attack, showing judgment as well as strength. Inside Lanka, he must exchange the scale of a giant leap for stealth, patience and observation.

He finds Sita in the Ashoka grove and witnesses her refusal of Ravana. Before approaching, he considers how to speak without frightening her or appearing to be another deception. The story of Rama, his answers to her questions and the signet ring work together to establish trust.

Sita gives Hanuman a token and messages for Rama. She discusses the risks of leaving on his back and asks how an army could cross the ocean. Hanuman then confronts Lanka’s forces, addresses Ravana and burns parts of the city after his tail is set alight. Concern that Sita may have been harmed makes him reassess his anger and verify her safety.

The mission ends when he returns and delivers her words. Rama’s desire to hear them again closes a book whose most spectacular physical achievement serves the restoration of communication between two separated people.

sections.heading: The war in Lanka and the return to Ayodhya
paragraphs: The allies gather at the ocean. Vibhishana, rejected after advising Ravana to return Sita, asks Rama for refuge. The camp debates the risk before Rama receives him. Nala directs the construction of a bridge, and the forces cross to Lanka.

[Yuddha Kanda](/ramayana/yuddha-kanda) contains a long war of reversals: extraordinary weapons, injured leaders, deception, healing and renewed battles. Kumbhakarna fights despite recognizing his brother’s error. Indrajit uses illusion and concealment before Lakshmana defeats him. Hanuman repeatedly helps save the wounded. Ravana finally falls to Rama.

The account then gives attention to funeral rites and the grief of Ravana’s household. Sita’s meeting with Rama brings another ordeal rather than immediate domestic peace. She protests his public words and enters the fire; Agni returns her unharmed and affirms her fidelity. Rama’s subsequent explanation in terms of public recognition remains part of the passage and of the debate it has generated.

The return journey retraces places associated with the exile. Hanuman brings news to Bharata, who prepares the welcome. Rama is crowned in Ayodhya. This completes the exile and gives the sixth book its great moment of restoration.

sections.heading: What the seventh book tells after the homecoming
paragraphs: [Uttara Kanda](/ramayana/uttara-kanda) first returns to earlier histories: Ravana’s family and conquests, and Hanuman’s childhood. It then continues Rama’s reign. Public suspicion about Sita leads him to order her removal from the kingdom, despite the earlier affirmation of her fidelity. Valmiki receives her, and Lava and Kusha are born and raised in the hermitage.

The book contains Shatrughna’s campaign against Lavana and several stories about rulers, sages and the consequences of conduct. It also includes the killing of Shambuka, an episode whose explanation through social hierarchy has drawn sustained criticism. A guide to the seven-book text should identify that episode rather than omit it because it is difficult.

Lava and Kusha recite the Ramayana before Rama at the royal sacrifice. Sita is called to appear, makes a final declaration and returns to the Earth. The ending does not restore her to palace life. Later chapters narrate Lakshmana’s departure, arrangements for the next generation and Rama’s final journey toward the Sarayu.

The seventh book’s textual history is debated in scholarship. This guide includes it as part of the received epic and states when its account is being used. Readers can recognize its place in tradition while examining how the text developed.

sections.heading: The questions that hold the story together
paragraphs: Dharma is often translated as duty or righteousness, but the epic does not reduce it to one instruction that settles every situation. Rama’s obligation to his father conflicts with what his mother and brother want him to do. Sita questions armed intervention in the forest. Vali questions the manner of his death. These exchanges invite the reader to examine reasons as well as outcomes.

Promises bind people across distance. Bharata’s sandals, Rama’s ring and Sita’s ornament are material signs through which an absent person remains present to another. They are not interchangeable symbols: one concerns rule, another the identity of a messenger, and another the credibility of news from captivity.

Kingship is judged through listening and through consequences. Dasharatha’s private promise changes the succession. Ravana’s refusal of unwelcome counsel destroys those around him. Rama’s concern with public opinion later divides his household. The text repeatedly asks who bears the cost of a ruler’s decision.

Devotion appears through concrete acts: Lakshmana’s service, Bharata’s refusal to take possession, Jatayu’s resistance and Hanuman’s work as a messenger. Later traditions develop these into extensive teachings on bhakti. The narrative foundation is often a particular act of care performed under difficult conditions.

Grief is not evidence that the characters lack strength. Rama searches and laments; Tara speaks beside Vali; Mandodari mourns Ravana; Sita refuses to surrender her judgment under pressure. Their emotional lives are part of what the poem asks readers to hear.

sections.heading: Familiar details that need their own source labels
paragraphs: Many people first meet the Ramayana through a television series, a family story, a local performance or the Ramcharitmanas. That is a valid entry point, but familiarity does not identify a detail’s textual source.

For example, the forest departure scene used in our Aranya guide does not include Lakshmana drawing a protective line. The Shabari chapter does not narrate her tasting every berry. The Bala account of Ahalya is not simply the familiar image of a woman turned into a stone. The bridge passage emphasizes Nala and the collective work of the vanaras rather than a universal claim about inscribed floating stones.

These distinctions are invitations to read more closely, not a ranking of the value of different traditions. A later story can be important to devotion and still require its own attribution. The same care applies to RudraNāda’s music: a song can imaginatively express a character’s feelings without claiming to translate a speech from Valmiki.

The existing article [Why Did Hanuman Forget His Powers?](/articles/why-hanuman-forgot-his-powers-jambavan-ramayana) demonstrates the method. It distinguishes Jambavan’s reminder in Kishkindha from the account of the curse in Uttara and separates both from a modern interpretation about discovering one’s potential.

sections.heading: The Ramayana in festivals and everyday devotion
paragraphs: [Rama Navami](/festivals/rama-navami) celebrates Rama’s birth. [Dussehra](/festivals/dussehra), in many Rama-centred traditions, remembers the defeat of Ravana. [Diwali](/festivals/diwali) is associated in many North Indian tellings with the return to Ayodhya, while the wider festival has other regional and religious meanings as well.

[Hanuman Jayanti](/festivals/hanuman-jayanti) belongs to Hanuman’s living devotional traditions, whose dates and observances vary. The Ramayana also opens onto stories associated with Ganga, sages and other deities. These connections help readers move between a continuous epic and the annual occasions through which parts of it are remembered.

Festival guides and narrative guides have different jobs. The former explain observances, dates and regional practice. The latter locate events within a text. Linking them should make that difference clear instead of presenting every modern festival detail as a verse from the epic.

sections.heading: Where should you begin?
paragraphs: For a first reading, begin with the seven-book story above and then follow the Kandas in order. The transitions matter: Maricha’s first encounter with Rama precedes the golden deer, Jatayu’s death prepares the meeting with Sampati, and Bharata’s waiting gives the homecoming its emotional force.

If Hanuman brought you here, begin with his first meeting with Rama in Kishkindha and then read Sundara. If you want to understand the family’s decisions, give Ayodhya Kanda time. If you are interested in Sita, follow her speech across the books rather than limiting her story to abduction and rescue.

Use the chapter-range map on each page to move into the source. Check the edition note before comparing a sarga number from somewhere else. The maps cover the main numbered sequence, while the Uttara guide also calls out the supplementary groups in its chosen translation.

There is no need to decide every interpretive question before reading. Start with what happens, listen to what different characters say about it, and keep the text’s statements separate from the meaning you draw from them. That approach leaves room for devotion and for careful inquiry.

characters: Rama
Son of Dasharatha and Kausalya; Sita’s husband
The exile whose search becomes a war, and the ruler whose obligations remain difficult after victory.
Sita
Janaka’s daughter; Rama’s wife
A speaking and deciding presence through marriage, exile, captivity, reunion and the later separation.
Lakshmana
Son of Dasharatha and Sumitra; Rama’s brother
Companion in exile, protector and warrior, repeatedly caught between affection and obedience.
Bharata
Son of Dasharatha and Kaikeyi; Rama’s brother
Rejects the advantage obtained through Rama’s exile and governs in his name.
Shatrughna
Son of Dasharatha and Sumitra; Bharata’s close companion
Supports Bharata and receives a sustained role in the campaign against Lavana in Uttara Kanda.
Hanuman
Sugriva’s minister and Rama’s messenger
Brings learning, judgment, strength and devotion to the work of finding Sita.
Sugriva and Vali
Brothers in conflict over Kishkindha
Their struggle brings Rama into a new alliance and a difficult dispute about justice.
Tara and Angada
Vali’s wife and son
Their counsel, grief and future make the consequences of Vali’s death visible.
Ravana
Ruler of Lanka; brother of Vibhishana and Kumbhakarna
Abducts Sita, rejects counsel and carries his kingdom into war.
Vibhishana
Ravana’s brother
Urges the return of Sita, seeks refuge with Rama and later rules Lanka.
Jatayu and Sampati
Brothers whose histories connect the forest and the sea
Jatayu resists the abduction; Sampati gives the search party its destination.
Valmiki, Lava and Kusha
Poet, teacher and the young singers of the epic
Connect Rama’s lived story with its preservation and performance.

questions.question: Who wrote the Ramayana?
questions.answer: Indian tradition attributes the Sanskrit Ramayana to Valmiki. This guide follows that epic while identifying its editions and distinguishing it from later retellings.

questions.question: What are the seven Kandas in order?
questions.answer: Bala, Ayodhya, Aranya, Kishkindha, Sundara, Yuddha and Uttara. Each Kanda is a book divided into sargas, or chapters.

questions.question: Is the Valmiki Ramayana the same as the Ramcharitmanas?
questions.answer: No. Valmiki’s work is a Sanskrit epic. Tulsidas’s Ramcharitmanas is a much later devotional work in Awadhi. They share a broad story but differ in structure, emphasis and narrative details.

questions.question: How long is Rama’s exile?
questions.answer: Kaikeyi demands fourteen years of forest exile in Ayodhya Kanda. Bharata’s waiting and Rama’s eventual return are structured around the completion of that period.

questions.question: Why does this guide include Uttara Kanda?
questions.answer: It belongs to the received seven-book text. The guide also explains scholarly discussion of its later textual development and identifies events that come specifically from it.

questions.question: Is this the full text of the Valmiki Ramayana?
questions.answer: No. It is a detailed reading guide with original summaries, character explanations, chapter-range maps and links to the source texts. It does not reproduce the complete Sanskrit epic or a full translation.
